content: Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted viral infection that affects the skin or mucous membranes of the genital area. It is primarily caused by two types of herpes simplex viruses: HSV-2 and HSV-1. HSV-2 is the most common cause of genital herpes, while HSV-1, which typically causes oral herpes (cold sores), can also infect the genital area through oral-genital contact. Many individuals infected with HSV-2 may never experience noticeable symptoms or may have very mild symptoms that are mistaken for other skin conditions, such as insect bites. However, when symptoms do occur, especially during the first outbreak, they can be severe. The initial outbreak typically occurs within two weeks of exposure to the virus. Systemic symptoms during the first outbreak may include: Loss of appetite Fever General malaise (a feeling of being unwell) Muscle aches, particularly in the lower back, buttocks, thighs, or knees Genital symptoms often involve the appearance of small, painful blisters filled with clear or straw-colored fluid. These blisters may occur: In women: on the outer vaginal lips (labia), inside the vagina, on the cervix, around the anus, or on the thighs and buttocks In men: on the penis, scrotum, around the anus, or on the thighs and buttocks In both sexes: on the tongue, mouth, eyes, gums, lips, fingers, or other parts of the body Before the blisters appear, individuals may experience tingling, burning, itching, or pain at the site where the blisters will form. When the blisters rupture, they leave shallow, painful ulcers that eventually crust over and heal within 7 to 14 days or longer. Other symptoms that may occur include: Enlarged and tender lymph nodes in the groin during an outbreak Painful urination Vaginal discharge in women, or in some cases, difficulty emptying the bladder, which may require catheterization Recurrent outbreaks can occur weeks or months after the initial episode. These subsequent outbreaks are usually less severe and shorter in duration. Over time, the frequency of outbreaks may decrease. However, once infected, the virus remains in the body, hiding in nerve cells in a dormant state (latency). The infection can reactivate at any time, leading to new outbreaks. Triggers for reactivation may include: Fatigue Genital irritation Menstruation Physical or emotional stress Trauma to the affected area The frequency of outbreaks varies widely, ranging from once a year to nearly continuous symptoms. Recurrent infections tend to be milder in men than in women. Herpes simplex virus is transmitted through direct contact with an infected person’s skin, mouth, or genital secretions. Transmission is most likely during active outbreaks when visible sores or blisters are present. However, the virus can also be spread when no symptoms or sores are visible, as the infected person may still shed the virus. This makes it possible for someone who is unaware of their infection to transmit the virus to others. Genital HSV-2 infections are more common in women (approximately 1 in 4 women) than in men (approximately 1 in 8 men). When to Seek Medical Care You should contact a healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of genital herpes, such as sores, fever, headache, vomiting, or widespread symptoms during or after an outbreak. Additionally, seek medical attention if you are unable to urinate. Diagnosis Herpes can be diagnosed through tests performed on skin sores or blisters. These tests are particularly useful during the first outbreak or in pregnant women with symptoms of genital herpes. Diagnostic methods include: Viral culture: Fluid from a blister or open sore is tested for the herpes simplex virus. Results are typically available within 2-3 days and are most accurate during the first outbreak. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): This test detects small amounts of viral DNA in fluid from a blister and is the most accurate method for confirming the presence of the herpes virus. Blood tests: These tests measure antibody levels to the herpes virus and can determine if someone has been infected, even if they have never had an outbreak. Treatment There is no cure for genital herpes, but antiviral medications can help manage the condition. These medications, such as acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir, can reduce pain and discomfort during outbreaks and promote faster healing of sores. They are most effective during the first outbreak but can also be used for recurrent episodes. For recurrent outbreaks, starting antiviral medication at the first sign of symptoms (e.g., tingling, burning, or itching) can help shorten the duration of the outbreak. For individuals with frequent outbreaks, daily suppressive therapy with antiviral medications can reduce the frequency and severity of outbreaks and lower the risk of transmitting the virus to others. Pregnant women may be treated with antiviral medications during the last month of pregnancy to reduce the risk of an outbreak during delivery. If an outbreak occurs at the time of delivery, a cesarean section (C-section) is recommended to prevent transmission to the baby. Possible side effects of antiviral medications include: Fatigue Headache Nausea and vomiting Rash Seizures Tremors Home Care To manage herpes sores at home: Avoid wearing nylon or synthetic underwear, pantyhose, or pants. Opt for loose-fitting cotton garments instead. Gently cleanse the affected area with soap and water. Warm baths may help relieve pain, but it is important to keep the blisters dry afterward. If a sore becomes infected with bacteria, consult your doctor about the need for antibiotics. Complications Pregnant women with active genital herpes infections at the time of delivery may transmit the virus to their newborns. The risk is highest if the mother is newly infected during pregnancy. Babies born to mothers infected during pregnancy are at risk for premature birth, brain infections (e.g., meningitis or encephalitis), chronic skin infections, severe developmental delays, or death. The risk of severe infection is lower in recurrent outbreaks, but it is highest when an outbreak occurs during delivery. In rare cases, herpes infections can involve the brain, eyes, esophagus, liver, spinal cord, or lungs, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with AIDS, undergoing chemotherapy, or taking high doses of steroids. Individuals with active herpes infections who engage in sexual contact with an HIV-positive partner are at increased risk of contracting HIV. Prevention The most effective way to prevent genital herpes is to avoid all sexual contact, including oral sex. Alternatively, being in a long-term, mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who has been tested and is not infected with herpes is another preventive measure. Condoms are the best protection against genital herpes during sexual activity with an infected partner. Latex condoms should be used consistently and correctly during all sexual contact, even when no sores or blisters are visible. Female condoms have also been shown to reduce the risk of transmission. Note that animal membrane condoms (e.g., sheepskin) do not provide protection against herpes, as the virus can pass through them. Individuals with genital herpes should inform their partners about their condition, even if they are asymptomatic. Experimental vaccines for herpes are under development but are not yet widely available.
